clue.text: Perhaps Mr Owl ate my metal worm?

definitions.text: Perhaps Mr Owl ate my metal worm?

blocks.clueFragment: Mr Owl ate my metal worm
blocks.note: surface reading: a nonsense tale of a bird eating a metal worm
setter's reading: the quoted sentence is an example of a phrase that reads the same backwards as forwards

explanation.surface: A whimsical scene of an owl gobbling up a mechanical worm.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the quoted words letter by letter from the end and they come out identical; 'Perhaps' tells you the sentence is just one example of the type.
explanation.definitionFit: A word or sentence that reads identically in both directions is the term for this kind of letter-symmetrical phrase.

clue.text: Religious leader burst bubble at last

indicators.note: 'at last' points to the final position, so only the closing letter of the word is used

blocks.note: to burst is to pop
final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A cleric pricks somebody's bubble in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Burst bubble' reads as one phrase, but 'burst' is a verb on its own and 'bubble at last' supplies one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The head of the Roman Catholic Church holds the title, making him the most prominent clerical figure.

clue.text: Spooner’s pipe poor as weapon

indicators.note: Rev Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of words, so the initial sounds here trade places

blocks.note: a bong is a water pipe; it takes the opening L sound of the next word
low means poor in quality; it takes the opening B sound of the previous word

explanation.surface: Someone's smoking pipe is so bad it might as well be used to fight with.
explanation.walkthrough: BONG LOW becomes LONG BOW when the B and L sounds change places.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall English archery bow used to devastating effect at Agincourt is a classic medieval arm.

clue.text: Naturalist not working for charitable organisation

indicators.note: something working is being operated or processed, so these letters are worked into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An unemployed nature expert ends up doing charity work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not working' looks like a single phrase meaning idle, but 'not' is fodder and 'working' alone signals the rearrangement. The National Trust is the British charity that looks after historic houses and countryside.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a registered British conservation charity that preserves stately homes, gardens and coastline for the public.

clue.text: Check two rivers for animal

blocks.note: to rein in is to check or restrain
the Dee, a river in Scotland and in Wales, plus R, the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: An inspector checks a pair of rivers looking for wildlife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Check' reads as inspect, but here it means restrain, as you would a horse.
explanation.definitionFit: This antlered Arctic deer is a species of mammal, so the general word covers it as an example.

clue.text: Chap taking pee in wood?

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a chap is a man
the letter P is spelt 'pee'

explanation.surface: A man relieving himself among the trees.
explanation.walkthrough: The vulgar surface is a decoy: 'pee' is just the name of the letter P.
explanation.definitionFit: The timber of this tree is a hardwood used for furniture and floors, so it names a type of lumber.

clue.text: One’s served hot stuff

blocks.note: first meaning: a course of food brought to the table
second meaning: an attractive person

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a waiter bringing something spicy; the second phrase is slang for a good-looking person.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a prepared item of food and is also informal slang for a sexy, attractive person.

clue.text: Document website miser owns

indicators.note: what a phrase owns it holds within it, so the letters sit inside the words

blocks.note: runs across the two words

explanation.surface: A tight-fisted person's online property is recorded on paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Document' looks like a noun, but it is the verb: to record in detail.
explanation.definitionFit: To list things one by one in writing is to record each item, which is what documenting them means.

clue.text: Admit NHS is unusually disorganised

indicators.note: unusually means not in the normal way, so the letters appear in an abnormal order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A complaint that the health service is in chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' looks like the verb joining the parts but belongs in the fodder. The NHS is Britain's National Health Service.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done haphazardly, sometimes succeeding and sometimes failing, lacks planning and order.

clue.text: Beer perhaps containing old wine

indicators.note: to contain is to hold within, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: beer is an example of a drink served by the pint
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A glass of ale with some vintage wine mixed in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' marks beer as an example of what fills the measure, not as the measure itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Pinot is a grape family (noir, grigio, blanc) and the red or white made from it.

clue.text: Reckless rascal seen with dirty books

blocks.note: an imp is a mischievous child
dirty jokes are rude
NT is the New Testament, a set of books

explanation.surface: A careless rogue spotted carrying smutty reading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Books' in crosswords is often OT or NT, the Old or New Testament.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting without care or thought for consequences is unwise, which is what lacking prudence means.

clue.text: A French mature Brie at last judged “perfect”

indicators.note: 'at last' refers to the end, so only the final letter is used

blocks.note: un is French for 'a'
mature means grown-up
final letter of the cheese's name
judged means assessed

explanation.surface: A ripe French cheese is finally declared flawless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mature Brie' looks like a description of the cheese, but 'mature' is a separate piece and Brie only gives its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Unadulterated means pure and complete, with nothing added, so it fits 'perfect' in the sense of utter or absolute.

clue.text: Lie to baron fighting with old family member

indicators.note: letters in a fight are thrown about and scrambled into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone deceives a nobleman who is feuding with an elderly relative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'old' looks like it describes the family member, but it is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A person related by birth rather than marriage is a kin member of your family.

clue.text: Led in by itinerant, everyone entering cul de-sac

indicators.note: an itinerant wanders from place to place, so the letters roam into a new order
to enter is to go inside, so one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: taken as written
everyone means all

explanation.surface: A wandering guide leads a group into a dead-end street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'itinerant' looks like a noun for the guide, but it is the anagram signal for the three words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A dead-end passage with no way through is a closed street, and figuratively a fruitless course of action.

clue.text: Unhappy with quality? This won’t float your boat

blocks.note: feeling low is feeling sad
as in a diamond 'of the first water', the highest quality

explanation.surface: Someone dissatisfied with a product that fails to excite them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Float your boat' is an idiom for pleasing someone, but here it is taken literally: a shallow tide can strand a vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: When the tide is out there may be too little depth to keep a vessel afloat, so the phrase works literally.

clue.text: Mother accepting employment in the Louvre, perhaps

indicators.note: to accept is to take in, so one piece is held inside the other

blocks.note: mum is an informal word for mother
employment of a tool is its use

explanation.surface: A mother takes a job at the famous Paris gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Employment' suggests a job, but here it means use, as in putting something to use.
explanation.definitionFit: The Louvre in Paris is an example of a public collection of art and antiquities on display.

clue.text: Oil treated sore knee

indicators.note: something treated is processed or worked on, so the letters are reworked into another order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Rubbing ointment into an aching joint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oil treated' reads as a remedy applied to the knee; 'Oil' is actually the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a paraffin fuel distilled from petroleum, burned in lamps and jet engines.

clue.text: Deny wife’s being released from famous prison

indicators.note: someone released from a place leaves it, so a letter departs from the longer word

blocks.note: Newgate was a notorious London jail
W is the abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: A man refuses to accept that his wife is getting out of jail.
explanation.walkthrough: Newgate was a London prison for over seven centuries, closed in 1902; remove its W.
explanation.definitionFit: To negate something is to nullify it or say it is not true, which is to contradict or refute it.

clue.text: On vacation, has put up with a week going after game bird

indicators.note: a vacated place is emptied, so the word loses its interior and keeps its outer letters
in a down entry, putting something up lifts it bottom to top, so its letters run in reverse
going after means following, so this group is placed behind the next one

blocks.note: Go is a Japanese board game
first and last letters of the word
taken as written
WK is the abbreviation for week

explanation.surface: A holidaymaker spends a week hunting pheasant or grouse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game bird' looks like the definition, but 'game' is the board game and only 'bird' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A goshawk is a large hawk, a bird of prey used in falconry.

clue.text: Upset when one becomes European? Calm down!

indicators.note: when one thing becomes another it is swapped out, so a letter is exchanged for a different one

blocks.note: to upset is to distress
the Roman numeral for one
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: Someone is anxious about changing nationality and is told to relax.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the I in the word for upset with an E.
explanation.definitionFit: To destress is to relax and shed tension, which is what calming down involves.

clue.text: Choose artist, a complex woman?

blocks.note: to elect is to choose
RA is a Royal Academician

explanation.surface: Picking a painter who turns out to be a complicated woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complex' suggests complicated, but it is the psychological term: the Electra complex, named after the Greek heroine. RA stands for Royal Academician.
explanation.definitionFit: Electra, the mythical Greek princess who avenged her father, gave her name to a theory in psychology.

clue.text: A sailor lacking refinement reported for physical test

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so we want the sound rather than the spelling

blocks.note: a salt is an old sailor and coarse means unrefined

explanation.surface: A rough-mannered seaman is written up during a fitness exam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Salt' (an old salt) is a crossword favourite for a sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: An obstacle circuit used in military training tests strength, stamina and agility.

clue.text: Temperature raised, showing a bit of leg

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for temperature
raised means high

explanation.surface: Things get hot when a little leg is on show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Temperature raised' reads as a fever, but the two words are separate pieces placed side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: The thigh is the upper section of the limb between hip and knee, so it is one part of it.

clue.text: Occasionally, golden eagle’s tail brings joy

indicators.note: occasionally means every so often, so only every other letter is kept
a tail is the back end, so only the final letter is used

blocks.note: first, third and fifth letters
final letter of the bird's name

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher is thrilled to glimpse a golden eagle's tail now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Golden eagle' looks like one bird, but the two words are treated separately.
explanation.definitionFit: Glee is great delight or happiness, often gleeful exultation, so it is a synonym.

clue.text: Apparently most ignorant, anyway

definitions.note: a whimsical reading of the answer as two words

blocks.note: first meaning: split into two words, it describes the person with the smallest amount of wisdom
second meaning: at any rate, at least

explanation.walkthrough: 'Apparently' warns that the first meaning comes from reading the word in two halves rather than a real sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Leastwise is a dated or dialect adverb meaning at least or at any rate, used just as anyway is.

clue.text: Stop Italy deporting all outsiders – that’s perfect

indicators.note: to deport is to expel, so every word loses its outermost letters and only the insides remain

blocks.note: inner letters of the word
inner letters of the country's name

explanation.surface: A call to end immigration from Italy, presented as an ideal outcome.
explanation.walkthrough: The political-sounding surface hides a simple trim: strip the first and last letter of each of the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words can mean complete or absolute, as in a total stranger or a perfect stranger.

clue.text: Couple living in largely OK estate

indicators.note: a resident lives inside a place, so the letters dwell within the words

blocks.note: spans the three words

explanation.surface: Two people living on a housing estate that's mostly fine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Couple' looks like a noun for two people; as the definition it is the verb meaning join together.
explanation.definitionFit: To yoke is to harness two animals together, or link things, which is to join or pair them.

clue.text: Worn-out after study, lawyers enthralled by article

indicators.note: to be enthralled is to be held captive, so these letters are held inside another piece

blocks.note: to read a subject at university is to study it
the Bar is the legal profession of barristers
the definite article

explanation.surface: Exhausted after long hours of revision, lawyers are captivated by a piece of writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' suggests a written piece; in crosswords it often means THE, A or AN.
explanation.definitionFit: Cloth worn so thin that the threads show is shabby and frayed, the literal sense of the adjective.
